content: Each year, approximately 358,000 women die during childbirth, with the majority of these deaths occurring in low-income countries. Over half of all maternal deaths happen within the first 24 hours after delivery, with severe postpartum bleeding being the leading cause. If postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is left untreated, it can result in hypovolemic shock, multi-organ failure, and maternal death within two to six hours, depending on the rate of blood loss and factors like pre-existing anemia. The review examined various methods for estimating blood loss during the third stage of labor. The most common method is visual estimation, where the birth attendant makes a quantitative or semi-quantitative assessment of the blood lost. Another method involves direct blood collection using a disposable, funnel-shaped plastic collector bag attached to a plastic sheet placed under the woman’s buttocks. Once bleeding stops, the blood in the bag can either be weighed (gravimetric technique) or measured directly using a calibrated scale. More advanced methods for blood loss measurement include determining hemoglobin concentration (Hb) through venous blood sampling and spectrophotometry. The dye dilution technique involves injecting a known quantity of dye into the vein and monitoring its plasma concentration after bleeding ceases. Similarly, nuclear medicine techniques use a radioactive tracer to measure its concentration after bleeding stops. While these advanced methods theoretically provide more accurate blood loss quantification, they are complex and not widely accessible in most clinical settings. The objective of this review was to evaluate alternative methods for estimating blood loss during the third stage of labor to help healthcare providers mitigate the adverse effects of postpartum hemorrhage following vaginal delivery. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, up to March 2018. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. The review included all randomized trials, including cluster-randomized trials, that evaluated methods for estimating blood loss after vaginal birth. Two authors independently assessed the trials for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, extracted data, and verified accuracy. The search yielded 62 reports, of which 12 were reviewed in full. Six trials were identified, with three included in the analysis, one excluded, and two ongoing. The included trials were conducted in hospital settings, with two in India and one large cluster-randomized trial across 13 European countries. The included trials were judged to have a low risk of bias. One cluster-randomized controlled trial in 13 Western European countries, involving over 25,000 women, compared direct measurement using calibrated drapes with visual estimation. This trial did not report on postpartum anemia (Hb < 9 mg/dL), blood loss > 500 mL, or maternal infection. Moderate-quality evidence suggested little to no difference between the two methods in terms of severe morbidity (e.g., coagulopathy, organ failure, ICU admission; adjusted risk ratio [RR] 0.82, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.48–1.39), blood transfusion risk (adjusted RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.46–1.46), use of plasma expanders (adjusted RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.42–1.42), or use of therapeutic uterotonics (adjusted RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.42–1.76). Another randomized controlled trial in India, involving 900 women, compared calibrated drapes (Excellent BRASSS-V Drape™) with the gravimetric technique. This trial did not report on postpartum anemia, severe morbidity, or maternal infection. High-quality evidence indicated that calibrated drapes improved the detection of blood loss > 500 mL compared to the gravimetric technique (RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.11–3.11). Low-quality evidence suggested little to no difference in blood transfusion risk between the two groups (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.06–15.94) or in the use of plasma expanders (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.19–2.35). High-quality evidence showed little to no difference in the use of therapeutic uterotonics (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.90–1.13), though the use of uterotonics was high in both groups (57% and 56%). Overall, the evidence from this review is insufficient to recommend one method over another for estimating blood loss after vaginal birth. The quality of evidence for predefined outcomes ranged from low to high, with downgrades due to imprecision. Many primary and secondary outcomes were not reported in the included trials. Future trials evaluating blood loss estimation methods should assess their impact on clinical maternal and neonatal outcomes, as well as their diagnostic accuracy. Well-designed, adequately powered randomized controlled trials are needed to correlate blood loss measurements with relevant clinical outcomes.
